title: Private Counter Factory with Step
problemStatement: Implement `createCounter(initialValue, step)` that encapsulates `initialValue` and `step` in a closure. It returns an object with `increment()`, `decrement()`, `getValue()`, and `reset()`.
interviewTrap: Exposing internal variables directly or allowing external mutation without getters/setters.

testCases.name: Independent counters maintain isolated states
testCases.testFn: const c1 = createCounter(0, 1); const c2 = createCounter(10, 2); c1.increment(); return [c1.getValue(), c2.getValue()];

testCases.name: Resets accurately to initial value
testCases.testFn: const c = createCounter(5, 2); c.increment(); c.increment(); c.reset(); return c.getValue();

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: A closure is the combination of a function bundled together with references to its surrounding lexical environment ([[Environment]]). A private counter factory uses closures to encapsulate state variables away from global scope, exposing only controlled modifier functions.
stepByStepWalkthrough: Initialize private variable `count = initial` and `stepValue = step` inside factory function.
Return an object containing accessor and mutator methods: `increment()`, `decrement()`, `reset()`, and `get()`.
Each method maintains a live reference to `count` and `stepValue` through the outer lexical environment record.
Outside consumers cannot read or mutate `count` directly, ensuring information hiding.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: In V8, variables referenced by an inner function that outlives the outer function call are allocated in a Heap Context rather than on the thread Call Stack. The returned methods hold an internal `[[Scopes]]` pointer referencing this Context object, preventing V8's Garbage Collector from reclaiming it.

complexity.time: O(1) for each method call (increment, decrement, reset, get).
complexity.space: O(1) heap allocation for the shared Lexical Environment context.

edgeCasesHandled: Custom initial values and custom step increments (e.g. initial=10, step=5).
Multiple independent counters maintain separate isolated lexical contexts without cross-contamination.
Reset restores initial count state cleanly.

specifications: ECMA-262 §9.1.1 Declarative Environment Records (Lexical scoping and closure mechanics)
MDN Web Docs: Closures & Lexical Scoping
verifiedRules: Inner functions retain access to outer declarative environment records across ticks.
Variables in a closure escape stack allocation and are preserved in heap-allocated context objects.

interviewCrossQuestions.question: Where are variables held in a closure stored in memory?
interviewCrossQuestions.answer: Variables captured by a closure that outlives its parent function are allocated on the V8 Heap inside a special internal `Context` object, NOT on the Call Stack. Stack memory is ephemeral and reclaimed immediately when a function returns. The Heap Context object is retained because the returned inner function holds a reference in its internal `[[Scopes]]` array, creating an active reachability path from GC roots.
interviewCrossQuestions.whyAsked: Tests whether you understand real memory allocation mechanics vs abstract lexical scope definitions.

interviewCrossQuestions.question: Can two different functions share the exact same closure context?
interviewCrossQuestions.answer: Yes. If an outer function defines multiple inner functions that reference outer variables, V8 allocates a single shared `Context` object for that scope. All inner functions point to that identical Context. Mutating a variable from one inner function is instantly observed by the other.
interviewCrossQuestions.whyAsked: Tests understanding of how engines bundle multiple closures from the same scope.

interviewCrossQuestions.question: How do closures relate to the classic for(var i=0; i<3; i++) setTimeout trap?
interviewCrossQuestions.answer: With `var`, there is only a single function-scoped variable binding for `i`. All three setTimeout callbacks close over the exact same variable reference. By the time the callbacks fire, the loop has completed and mutated `i` to 3. Replacing `var` with `let` creates a new lexical environment binding for `i` on every loop iteration, giving each callback its own distinct closed-over copy.
interviewCrossQuestions.whyAsked: The universal junior-to-mid litmus test for closure understanding.

interviewCrossQuestions.question: What is the [[Scopes]] internal property on a function object?
interviewCrossQuestions.answer: In V8 and Chromium DevTools, every function has a hidden internal slot `[[Scopes]]`. It contains a scope chain linked list: from the local closure Contexts, through module and script scopes, up to the Global scope. When resolving variable lookups, the engine walks this chain from nearest to furthest.
interviewCrossQuestions.whyAsked: Tests whether the candidate has inspected function internals using Chrome DevTools or Node inspect.

interviewCrossQuestions.question: Do modern JS engines keep unreferenced variables in a closure context?
interviewCrossQuestions.answer: No. Modern engines (V8, SpiderMonkey) perform Scope Analysis during AST parsing. Any variable declared in the outer scope that is NEVER referenced by any inner function is stripped and discarded from the heap Context. Only referenced variables are retained, optimizing heap memory usage.
interviewCrossQuestions.whyAsked: Checks if candidate understands V8 dead-code and scope pruning optimizations.

realWorldUseCases.description: Before ES2022 private class fields (#field), closures were the primary mechanism for true information hiding in JavaScript, preventing external consumers from tampering with internal state.
realWorldUseCases.codeSnippet: function createStore(initial) { let state = initial; return { getState: () => state, setState: (s) => { state = s; } }; }

realWorldUseCases.description: React hooks rely on closures to bind component render cycles to fiber nodes. Each render pass captures state and dispatchers within that render's functional closure.
realWorldUseCases.codeSnippet: const [count, setCount] = useState(0); // count is captured in component closure

realWorldUseCases.description: Utilities like `curry` and `debounce` use closures to accumulate arguments across multiple distinct invocations until threshold conditions are satisfied.
realWorldUseCases.codeSnippet: const add = a => b => a + b;

howToExplain.opening: A closure is a function bundled together with references to its surrounding lexical environment. It allows an inner function to retain access to variables from an outer scope even after that outer function has returned.
keyPoints: Functions in JS carry an internal [[Environment]] reference to their enclosing Lexical Environment Record.
Captured variables escape stack frame destruction and are allocated on the V8 Heap inside a Context object.
Multiple functions created in the same scope share the same closure Context.
Closures provide the foundation for private encapsulation, currying, and React hook state persistence.
howToExplain.closingImpression: Closures are not a special feature you opt into; in JavaScript, all functions are closures because they retain lexical scope references by default.
analogies: A closure is like taking a backpack with supplies from your hometown when you travel; even after leaving town, you still have everything you packed inside your backpack.

commonMistakes.mistake: Saying that closures copy variable values.
commonMistakes.why: Closures do NOT copy values; they capture live references to the binding in the environment record. If the variable mutates later, the closure reads the mutated value.
commonMistakes.correct: State that closures hold live references to outer variable bindings, not static snapshot copies.

commonMistakes.mistake: Thinking closures only exist when an inner function is returned.
commonMistakes.why: Any inner function referencing an outer variable forms a closure, even if passed as a callback to setTimeout or an event listener without being returned.
commonMistakes.correct: Explain that closure formation depends on lexical nesting and variable access, not the return statement.

followUpDeepDive.question: Explain the 'Eval Scope Leak' edge case in V8 closure optimization.
followUpDeepDive.answer: Normally V8 prunes unreferenced variables from heap Contexts. However, if a function contains a direct `eval()` call, V8 cannot predict at compile time which variables `eval` might access at runtime. Consequently, V8 is forced to deoptimize and retain ALL outer scope variables in the heap Context, potentially causing unintended memory retention.
followUpDeepDive.specReference: ECMA-262 §13.3.7.1 Direct Eval Arguments & V8 Scope Analysis
